She is holding back tears and she is losing. That is the entire content of the shot.
This is not crying. It is the fight not to cry, which is a different physical event: the body trying to suppress a response that is already underway. The tears are present before the shot begins. What we watch is the suppression failing by degrees, the turn it forces, and one small involuntary act of self-management afterwards.
In the first seconds she is holding two things at once: the tears, and his eyes. She can only manage one. The turn is what it costs her to keep managing the tears.
Once she is on the window she is alone with it. There is nothing to see out there. The window is somewhere to put her eyes.
Nothing lands cleanly. No expression arrives on a beat. Everything is continuous, involuntary and slightly behind itself.

"Look, somebody else got there first."
"Look" comes out a fraction softer and slower than the rest — the only piece of him in the sentence, a half-apology before the wall goes up. Then the rest arrives flat and quick, the exact cadence of a decision read from a desk, the words of his office coming out of his mouth. The flatness is deliberate armour, not indifference: as he says "first", the lower lids tighten a fraction and the jaw sets, because he is hearing his own working voice in his own kitchen. The torso comes forward a couple of centimetres as he starts to speak and stays there through the line. Small pause after, mouth staying parted, then closing.

"It isn't us. We don't decide."
This is the line that costs him most, because "us" and "we" are a lie he is standing inside. The first sentence goes out fast, almost defensive, a shade louder than line one — he is answering something she has not said. Then the tiny fracture: on "We don't decide" the voice drops and thins, the certainty draining out mid-phrase, the last word coming out with less air behind it than the ones before it. The brow draws in a millimetre and releases. One deeper intake before the line, the whole ribcage taking it. The shoulders drop a centimetre between the two sentences and the torso settles back with them, the armour slipping and being pulled back up — shoulders and spine lifting again by the end of the line. He is not convincing her. He is failing to convince himself, in front of her.

"Don't."
Not an order and not aggression. It is the smallest sound in the shot — quiet, close to breath, a man asking not to be pushed one more inch. His torso stops its drift entirely on the word — a half-second of genuine arrest, the only moment in the take where his body is truly still — and then resumes. Immediately after it the whole face gives half a millimetre — the outer corners of the eyes soften, the mouth stays open a beat too long — and then he takes it back and holds. The eyeline does not break.

THE HALL
A large hall inside an old hospital, converted for a mass programme. Pale institutional walls, scuffed. Worn vinyl floor. High ceiling with a scatter of fluorescent fittings — irregularly placed, not in a repeating grid, some off.
Along one side, a run of three or four service counters with glazed screens and small openings, each visibly different: different heights of paperwork stacked, different clutter, one with its shutter half down. NOT identical booths in a row.
Loose plastic chairs across the floor, not in neat rows: some in short irregular groups, some pulled out of line, some turned to face different directions, several occupied and several empty.
Retractable belt barriers on posts marking a queue lane toward the counters, the belts slack and one of them dropped.
A paper ticket dispenser. A small digital number display high on the wall.
Roughly FIFTY PEOPLE in the hall: standing, sitting, waiting, shuffling forward. Coats on, bags held, tickets in hands. A working room, busy and slow.
Nothing else: no posters, no health notices, no plants, no clock, no signage, no branding, no readable text anywhere.

WHAT IS HAPPENING — A ROUTINE HEALTH PROGRAMME
This plays as a mass public vaccination and registration drive. Everything about it is orderly and administrative.
People queue. They hold numbered tickets. They wait, shift their weight, look at their phones, look at nothing. Nobody is restrained, herded, pushed or forced. There are no guards, no uniforms except hospital scrubs behind the counters, no weapons, no barriers beyond the retractable belts.
The mood is BOREDOM, not fear. This is a long wait in a public building.
That ordinariness is the entire point.

SHOT 1 — THE HALL (0:00 to 0:04)
Handheld wide from inside the crowd, camera at chest height, in among the standing people rather than above them.
The frame is WIDE ACROSS: the hall stretches to the left and right of frame, full of people, and a plain wall closes the depth about eight metres back. No corridor, no vanishing point.
In the near foreground, out of focus and cutting into the lower third: the shoulder and back of the head of someone standing directly in front of the lens. They do not move away.
Beyond them, the crowd: perhaps thirty people visible, all seen as backs of heads, shoulders, coats and bags. Some standing, some seated in the irregular chairs. Not one face is resolved — the ones facing this way are too soft, too small, or turned. Every colour of coat is different. Every head is different.
Movement is slow and ambient: a few people shuffle forward, one steps sideways out of frame, someone shifts a bag from one hand to the other. No choreography, no synchronised movement, nobody crossing the frame dramatically.
The camera drifts slightly and corrects late, once. Focus is on the middle distance and hunts briefly at 0:02 before settling.
The frame is off-level and stays that way.
HARD CUT.

SHOT 2 — THE QUEUE (0:04 to 0:08)
Handheld medium, camera at chest height, positioned INSIDE the queue lane looking along it toward the counters.
The queue runs at an ANGLE across the frame, not straight away from the lens: it enters from one side, crosses the middle ground, and reaches the counters at the far side of frame. This angle is what prevents a receding line of repeating figures.
In the near foreground, out of focus: the back of the person immediately ahead in the queue, filling one side of the frame, coat and shoulder and the back of a head. They occupy a third of the image and block the sightline down the line.
Beyond them, perhaps fifteen people in the queue, seen from behind and at three-quarter rear: backs, shoulders, hands holding tickets, one arm scratching a neck. NOT ONE FACE resolved.
At the far end, one counter opening, and behind the glazed screen a pair of hands in blue nitrile gloves working on a forearm laid on the counter — small in frame, partly obstructed, not the subject. Whoever's arm it is, no face is shown.
The queue moves ONCE, a small collective shuffle forward of half a step, uneven and untidy: some people move, some do not, some move a beat later than others. Never in unison.
The camera is jostled slightly as the person in front moves, and reframes late. Focus stays on the middle of the queue.
The frame is off-level and stays that way.
END.

PERFORMANCE LOCK — NOBODY ACTS
No one performs an emotion. This is being recorded, not staged.
The crowd is bored and slow. Not afraid, not resigned, not staring meaningfully. People are waiting and their attention is on nothing.
Nobody looks at the camera. Nobody reacts to it. Nobody clears a path for it. Nobody performs for it.
Nobody speaks in a way that reads as directed at anyone: the ambience contains voices, but no conversation is legible and nobody is seen speaking clearly in frame.
Bodies move independently and at different rates. No two people move in sync at any moment. No wave of unified movement passes through the crowd.

PHYSICS
Real gravity, real mass, real material behaviour.
Standing bodies shift weight, rock slightly, and settle. People carrying bags counterbalance them.
Coats and heavy fabric hang with weight and crease; sleeves and hems move a beat behind the bodies.
The queue moves as a loose uneven chain, not as a block: the movement propagates person to person with gaps and lags.
Plastic chairs do not flex under weight. The belt barriers hang slack in shallow curves; one lies on the floor.
Paper tickets bend in fingers and hold a curl.
No floating bodies, no weightless objects, no frictionless feet, no rubbery CG motion, no game-engine crowd, no crowd moving as a single mesh.

LIGHTING
Available light only, and clearly so: overhead fluorescent, uneven, slightly green, with poor falloff. Some fittings are off, so parts of the hall are noticeably darker than others.
The scatter of fittings is IRREGULAR: not a repeating grid, not evenly spaced, not symmetrical.
Some parts of every frame are underlit and some are slightly hot. Nothing is shaped, nothing is added.
The light shifts slightly between the two shots because the operator has moved to a different part of the hall. The same room, the same fittings, unmatched coverage. That inconsistency is correct.
Within each shot the light does not change and does not flicker.
No window, no daylight visible.
No red light anywhere: no scanner, no beam, no laser, no indicator, no LED beyond the dim number display.
No theatrical front light, no beauty fill, no studio key, no rim light, no light from camera position, no golden grade, no coloured light, no vignette, no cinematic contrast.

SCENE CONTEXT
A vote is taken in a large international assembly chamber. Delegates cast their votes from consoles at their desks, small green and red lights come on across the tiered rows, the tally climbs on the display board above the podium, the result locks on APPROVED, and the entire chamber rises to applaud. Covered by the chamber's own house cameras.

FORMAT MODE
CONTROLLED MULTI-SHOT SEQUENCE, 15 seconds total. Five shots. HARD CUTS only at 0:04, 0:07, 0:09 and 0:12. Real-time motion.
The cuts are house-system switcher cuts between four fixed cameras already installed in the chamber. Every camera stays in the rear half of the room and faces forward toward the podium, so screen direction never reverses.
No fade, no crossfade, no dissolve, no transition effects. No subtitles, no music, no burned-in titles.

LOCATION MAP
The chamber is filmed from the rear. The podium wall is forward and screen-centre in every shot. Delegate rows are curved and tiered, facing forward toward the podium. The exit aisle runs along the screen-left side of the chamber in every shot.
Each delegate desk carries a gooseneck microphone, a small nameplate, and a flat voting console with three recessed buttons and a small indicator lamp above them.
Mounted high and centre on the podium wall is a large electronic vote display board.
Light comes from ceiling fixtures directly overhead, straight down, plus a weaker wash on the podium wall. Light direction is identical in all five shots.
Camera 1: elevated press platform, rear centre, 4 meters above floor, 25 meters from the podium wall, a dark press desk rail crossing the bottom edge of frame 1.2 meters from the lens.
Camera 2: fixed house camera, rear-left quadrant, 2.5 meters above floor, 9 meters from the nearest delegate row, angled forward and slightly down across the rows toward the podium.
Camera 3: fixed house camera, rear-left quadrant, 3 meters above floor, 20 meters from the podium wall, framed on the display board.
Camera 4: fixed house camera, rear-left quadrant, 2 meters above floor, 5 meters from a single delegate desk, angled forward and down onto the desk surface and voting console.

CONTINUITY LOCK ACROSS ALL CUTS
Same chamber, same delegates, same wardrobe, same overhead light direction, same screen-left aisle. The vote progresses continuously across the cuts and never resets: lit consoles stay lit, the tally never counts backward, the board result never changes once locked. No delegate teleports between shots. No new characters after a cut. No camera crosses the room axis.

OPTICS LOCK ACROSS ALL CUTS
No wide-angle lens character is used anywhere in this sequence. All architectural lines stay perfectly rectilinear. Absolutely no barrel distortion, no fisheye curve, no bowed horizon, no stretched or bulging figures at the frame edges, no circular vignette, no curved desk rows, no warped ceiling line. Natural human-eye geometry in every shot. Wider coverage is achieved only by the camera being farther away, never by a shorter lens.

PHYSICS
Bodies carry real mass in the chairs. Weight transfers through the hips before a delegate rises, hands press the desk edge for leverage, chairs rock backward and settle with hinge resistance.

Applause has real hand mass: palms meet with visible impact and rebound, arms carry inertia, sleeves and cuffs shift with each clap, no two people are in phase.

SCENE CONTEXT
A city square during a mass protest that has turned into a riot. A dense crowd pushes against a police line, a petrol bomb breaks on wet asphalt and spreads burning fuel across the ground, gas smoke drifts through the square. Covered by a professional news crew working inside the riot: one shoulder-mounted broadcast camera, one operator, one continuous assignment cut into four usable takes.

FORMAT MODE
CONTROLLED MULTI-SHOT SEQUENCE, 15 seconds total. Four shots. HARD CUTS only at 0:04, 0:08 and 0:11. Real-time motion.
All four shots come from the same camera and the same operator moving through the square during the same minute, so the image texture, lens character, exposure behaviour and operator body are identical across every cut. The cuts are edit points in news rushes, not different sources.
No fade, no crossfade, no dissolve, no transition effects. No subtitles, no music, no burned-in titles, no timecode, no station graphics.

LOCATION MAP

The crowd occupies the screen-left half of the square and pushes toward screen-right in every shot.
The police line holds the screen-right third: a solid wall of riot shields, helmets and visors formed across the square mouth, facing screen-left toward the crowd.
Between them, roughly 8 meters of open wet asphalt scattered with debris, broken glass, abandoned placards, and a burning patch of spilled fuel.

PHYSICS
Real body weight throughout. The head drop and the head lift move only the head and neck: his seat, his hips and his forearm on the table do not shift with them, and the chair takes no new load.
The head has mass: the neck lowers it against gravity with control and lifts it with effort, both decelerating on arrival, both settling with a hair of overshoot rather than locking.
Real facial musculature: the speech and the blinks travel through connected muscle groups and never read as a swapped mask. The jaw hinges properly, the cheeks and the beard move with it, the lips have thickness and wet contact, the throat and the sternocleidomastoid move as he speaks, as he breathes and as the head travels.
The blinks have real lid mechanics and real duration: the upper lid leads, the lower lid barely moves, the eye is fully covered for two or three frames and no longer.
Linen has cloth delay and real stiffness: it creases across the chest with each breath and releases a fraction later, gathers slightly at the collar as the neck bows and releases as it straightens, and the creases change slightly over the take rather than resetting.
Skin behaves as skin: pores, individual beard hairs and grey in the beard, fine creases at the outer eye corners, a faint sheen on the forehead and the bridge of the nose, the wet film on the eye.
All motion accelerates, travels and decelerates, always at 1x. No rubbery face, no CG morphing, no weightless head, no dreamlike or floaty motion, no jerky stop-start.

He seats the side straps of his tactical vest, bends forward to lace his boots, and pulls on his gloves. One continuous 20-second take on an 85mm prime, the camera creeping forward on an extremely slow dolly in. Observational documentary realism — a man putting on his gear, not a hero suiting up. His movements are fluid, unhurried and continuous throughout, never jerky and never stop-start.

Body. Human joint limits, human speed, human effort. The weight sits on the bench and stays there; the spine settles and re-settles under load, visible as gradual changes in the curve of the back. BREATHING drives the frame from the first frame to the last: a slow uneven cycle lifting and settling the shoulders, the collar and the shirt across the chest, visible while his head is up and while it is down. Across nine seconds he takes roughly three to four unequal breaths — one slightly deeper, the intervals not metronomic — and the cycle never syncs to a line, to the head drop, to the head lift or to a blink, and none of them is positioned to prepare a line.
THE HEAD is a real mass on a real neck. Whenever it is up it carries a slow low-frequency drift of a degree or two, arriving late, overshooting by a hair and settling, continuously and never repeating. Whenever it is down it still carries that drift, smaller. It also transmits the breathing: a fractional rise and fall with the chest. Outside the one scripted drop and the one scripted lift it never becomes a nod, a tilt or a turn.
THE TORSO makes the small postural corrections of a seated body: an almost imperceptible settling of weight, the spine adjusting a millimetre, one shoulder easing and returning. Once, around 8:20, there is a SINGLE tiny weight shift — the kind a body makes without noticing after a while in a chair — read only as a small settle through the shoulders and a shift of the shirt creases. It is not a lean, not a reposition, and it is not timed to anything.
THE SHOULDERS are not symmetrical and not locked: the right one sits lower because of the forearm on the table, and the trapezius on that side stays relaxed while the left does not. Both move with the breath, slightly out of step with each other. They round very slightly forward while the head is down and return as it comes up.
THE FACE has continuous minor life beneath the fixed expression: the small tensions and releases around the eyes and mouth that a resting face always has, the nostrils moving faintly with the breath, the throat moving with it above the collar. It is never a static mask and never a mask that swaps between poses.
HAIR AND CLOTH lag: the loose strand falling past the temple swings forward as the head goes down and back as it comes up, settling late both times; the linen at the shoulders and chest moves a fraction behind the body, never in perfect step with it.
FORBIDDEN: no looping cycle, no smooth sinusoidal drift, no CG head-bob, no locked-off frozen figure, no snapping between poses, no movement that lands on a word, no fidgeting, no restlessness, nothing that reads as an intention.

HIS ENTRANCE
He walks in from the RIGHT EDGE at an ordinary unhurried walking pace, two steps, and stops. It takes roughly one and a half seconds from the first sliver of him at the edge to fully stopped.
BECAUSE THE CAMERA IS LOW AND HE IS STANDING, WHAT ENTERS IS A FULL-HEIGHT COLUMN CUT AT THE CHIN. A tall dark mass crosses the frame edge from the right: first a blurred vertical edge, then the arm and sleeve, then the plate carrier and the gaiter, and at the very top the underside of the chin and the beard edge sliding in beneath the frame line. NOTHING ABOVE THE CHIN EVER ENTERS. His mouth, nose and eyes stay above the picture through the whole walk and after it.
He comes to rest one step in front of her, facing her, his weight settled. He does not stoop, does not lower himself, does not bend toward her, and does not tilt his head down far enough to bring his mouth or nose into frame. His head is angled down toward her, but the frame line is below that: only the chin and jaw register the angle.
He arrives with WEIGHT: the mass decelerates over the last half-step rather than stopping dead, and there is one small settle of the plate carrier as the weight comes down, the whole column dropping a centimetre and stopping, the chin at the top edge dropping with it. The gear swings faintly and comes to rest. Then he is still.
HE NEVER CROSSES HER. He does not pass in front of her face, does not occlude her at any point, does not continue toward frame left. He stops in his own third of the frame and her face is never blocked.
FORBIDDEN DURING THE ENTRANCE: no lunge, no rush, no looming down toward her, no crouching on arrival, no whip of movement, no dramatic shadow sweeping across her, no camera flinch, no rack focus onto him, no pause mid-step, no reframing to make room for him, and above all NO TILT UP TO FIND HIS FACE.

THE LIFT
SHE RAISES HER HEAD BECAUSE HE ARRIVES. The movement begins a fraction of a second after the first of him crosses the frame edge, and her eyes arrive on him at the moment he comes to rest. The two movements overlap: she is coming up while he is still coming in.
IT IS A LONG WAY UP AND IT ENDS OUT OF FRAME. Because he is standing and she is seated, the head does not simply lift: it goes back on the neck, the chin travelling up and the throat opening and lengthening, until she is looking steeply up at a face ABOVE THE TOP EDGE OF THE PICTURE. Her eyeline passes his visible chin and continues past the frame line. The travel is visibly greater than a level look would need.
It takes roughly one and a quarter seconds and it is CONTINUOUS. Not slow and not fast: the speed of a head coming up because something has entered the room, without hurry and without alarm. One movement, no stages, no pause halfway, no false start.
IT IS NOT A STARTLE. No snap, no jerk, no whip round, no flinch preceding it, no shoulders jumping. Her body does not move: her torso does not rise, her spine does not straighten, her shoulders do not square, her arms do not tighten on the child. She does not get up. Only the head comes up.
The chin travels up and slightly toward screen-right. The face rotates into the key from screen-left and becomes legible for the first time in the shot: the brow, then the eyes, then the full face, then the catchlight. At the top of the movement her eyes carry high in the sockets to hold a point above the frame.
Her eyes arrive on him at the very end of the movement, not before it: she does not look up first and lift the head after. The gaze arrives with the face.
It does not overshoot and it does not settle back. It arrives and stops, held, with only involuntary micro-motion after.
Her loose hair moves with delay and settles late; the strands falling across the side of her face trail behind the movement and come to rest across her cheek and jaw.
The rocking of the child does not pause, slow or quicken during the lift. The two motions are independent.
FORBIDDEN DURING THE LIFT: no gasp, no intake of breath, no dramatic reveal, no rise timed to a sound, no eyes opening as if waking, no hair pushed back, no expression changing as the face comes into view, no lifting of the body with the head, and no camera tilt following her gaze upward.

THE FACE
She is frightened. The fear is present in the body and is never played on the face.
Physically present and required: pallor under a faint damp sheen on the forehead, the nose and the upper lip; the exhausted drawn quality of <<<image_2>>>; loose strands of hair across the side of her face and jaw; breathing shallow and high in the chest, visible in the nostrils and at the exposed throat above the fleece collar; a fine involuntary tremor at the jaw and in the muscle beside the mouth, small enough to almost miss; eyes locked high on a point above the frame and not blinking longer than is comfortable; the eyes wet with strain, but no tear forms and nothing runs; the mouth closed, lips slightly parted only enough to breathe.
Once the head is up her face does not change for the rest of the take. Nothing arrives, nothing resolves, nothing escalates.
NOTHING READABLE PASSES OUT OF THIS FACE: no plea, no appeal, no apology, no defiance, no anger, no submission, no attempt to communicate. She is not asking him for anything. She is waiting.
Once her eyes are on him she does not look away for a single frame. She does not lower her gaze, does not look down at the child, does not look into the lens.

HEAD MOVEMENT — LIVING, NOT STILL
Her head is never frozen, before the lift or after it. It carries continuous involuntary micro-motion for all five seconds, and that micro-motion is separate from the lift.
Her rocking of the child travels up through her body and moves her head with it: a small slow oscillation, unchanging in speed and amplitude from the first frame to the last. It continues through his entrance and through the lift, riding on top of them. It never slows, never quickens, never pauses, and is never used as a reaction.
Her shallow high breathing moves the head faintly on top of that, faster and less regular than the rocking, the two motions overlapping without falling into rhythm.
After the lift there is a fine unsteadiness in the neck from holding the head tilted back at a strained upward angle while carrying the child's weight: tiny corrections, arriving late, overshooting by a hair and settling. This strain is greater than it would be at a level eyeline and is visible in the throat.
Her eyes hold his position through all of it, compensating for the movement exactly as real eyes do on a moving head. THE MICRO-MOTION NEVER CARRIES HER GAZE OFF SCREEN-RIGHT AND NEVER LOWERS IT.
His column, once he has stopped, carries the involuntary motion of a standing body under load: the slow low-frequency sway of the mass, the plate carrier lifting and settling with each breath, the pouches shifting a millimetre, the chin and beard edge at the top of frame moving a hair with it. It is never a gesture, never a turn, and it never descends toward her. His jaw never opens: he does not speak and his mouth is not in frame anyway.
FORBIDDEN: no second lift, no lowering after the lift, no nod, no shake, no tilt used as meaning, no head turning away, no chin lift beyond the end position, no cocking, no head movement that lands on anything. No looping cycle, no smooth sinusoidal drift, no CG head-bob, no locked-off frozen head, no snapping between poses.

PHYSICS
Real gravity, real mass, real material behaviour.
He is a loaded body walking upright: the plate carrier is a rigid mass that rides on the torso and lags a beat behind each step, riding up and settling as the weight transfers, and that transfer is fully visible because the torso is what is in frame. The walk decelerates over the last half-step and there is one small downward settle at the stop, absorbed through the knees and read as a drop of the whole column, chin included. The gear swings a centimetre and comes to rest.
Her head is a real mass on a real neck: it accelerates and decelerates smoothly through the lift, arrives with a fraction of inertia and settles rather than locking. The tendons and the line of the throat change and stay changed as the head holds back. Hair follows late.
The child has infant weight against her chest, held as in <<<image_2>>>, and settles very slightly with each rocking cycle. The wrapped cloth holds coarse folds and moves with delay. The child is not disturbed by either event.
Her padded jacket is bulky and stiff: it holds its own volume, creases and bunches at the collar as her head goes back, the fabric compressing at the back of her neck and lagging behind the movement, the fleece deforming against her throat.
Her seated weight is real: she is settled low on the mattress edge and does not shift on it.
No floating motion, no weightless infant, no rubbery cloth, no CG skin, no gliding walk, no snapping between poses.

He is a man saying the sentence that killed his own child, in the flat vocabulary he uses at work, to the one person who knows he is part of the machine that wrote it. He has already lost the child. He has not yet lost her, and he can feel it going.

LINE-BY-LINE DELIVERY
"Look, somebody else got there first."
"Look" comes out a fraction softer and slower than the rest — the only piece of him in the sentence, a half-apology before the wall goes up. Then the rest arrives flat and quick, the exact cadence of a decision read from a desk, the words of his office coming out of his mouth. The flatness is deliberate armour, not indifference: as he says "first", the lower lids tighten a fraction and the jaw sets, because he is hearing his own working voice in his own kitchen. Small pause after, mouth staying parted, then closing.

"It isn't us. We don't decide."
This is the line that costs him most, because "us" and "we" are a lie he is standing inside. The first sentence goes out fast, almost defensive, a shade louder than line one — he is answering something she has not said. Then the tiny fracture: on "We don't decide" the voice drops and thins, the certainty draining out mid-phrase, the last word coming out with less air behind it than the ones before it. The brow draws in a millimetre and releases. One deeper intake before the line; the shoulders drop a centimetre between the two sentences, the armour slipping and being pulled back up. He is not convincing her. He is failing to convince himself, in front of her.

"Don't."
Not an order and not aggression. It is the smallest sound in the shot — quiet, close to breath, a man asking not to be pushed one more inch. He says it because she has started to move and if she moves he will not hold. The lips barely part; the word is almost swallowed. Immediately after it the whole face gives half a millimetre — the outer corners of the eyes soften, the mouth stays open a beat too long — and then he takes it back and holds. The eyeline does not break.

He is the last one in the row and there is nobody after him. Both his parents have already been through it, in front of him, and he has watched. So unlike them he has nothing to be already looking past: the only thing in these ten seconds is his own result.

He is twenty and this is the first time the machine has been pointed at him with his family watching.
